summary: John Denver was a folk-pop singer and songwriter whose warm voice and outdoor themes made him one of the best-selling acts of the 1970s.
know: He wrote "Leaving on a Jet Plane," which Peter, Paul and Mary took to number one in 1969.
Before going solo he sang with the Chad Mitchell Trio.
He won the CMA Entertainer of the Year award in 1975.

influencedBy.why: The Kingston Trio's clean, harmony-based folk pop was the model for the folk groups he started in.
Peter, Paul and Mary shared his producer Milt Okun and turned his song into a hit, launching his career.
Seeger's singalong folk and nature songs set the template for Denver's earnest, audience-friendly style.
Dylan's success made room for folk singers to write their own material, which Denver did from the start.

cousins.why: Another clean-voiced 1970s crossover star who moved easily between country and pop radio.
Gentle, story-driven crossover songs that topped both country and pop charts.

summary: Charley Crockett is a Texas singer who blends honky-tonk, blues and soul into a deliberately old-fashioned sound and releases records at a fast clip.
know: He spent years busking in places like the New Orleans French Quarter and the New York subway before recording.
He released a full tribute album to the Texas honky-tonk singer James Hand.
He runs his own label, Son of Davy, and often puts out more than one album a year.
keyAlbums: 10 for Slim: Charley Crockett Sings James Hand

influencedBy.why: Haggard's working-man honky-tonk is the clearest model for Crockett's songwriting and vocal phrasing.
Western swing rhythms and Texas dance-hall feel run through many of his records.
He works in the plain, lonesome honky-tonk tradition that Hank Williams defined.
His blues-leaning sides draw on the Texas country-blues style of Lightnin' Hopkins.
Willie's Texas independence and conversational phrasing are an audible touchstone.
Outlaw-era Waylon is a reference point for his lean, guitar-driven arrangements.

cousins.why: A fellow Texan who revives vintage soul with the same respect for old recording sounds.
Rough-edged Texas songs built for small rooms and road stories.

summary: Bo Burnham is a comedian and songwriter who went from teenage YouTube videos to the self-made special Inside, mixing jokes with sharp pop songwriting.
know: He started posting comic songs to YouTube in 2006 while still in high school.
He wrote and directed the film Eighth Grade in 2018.
His song "All Eyes on Me" from Inside won a Grammy.

influencedBy.why: Lehrer's witty piano songs are the classic model for the kind of comedy music Burnham writes.
Weird Al showed that comedy songs could be built with real pop craft.
Newman's ironic, character-driven piano songs are close kin to Burnham's sharper material.
The Conchords' genre-hopping musical comedy was a contemporary model for Burnham's style parodies.

cousins.why: Another comedian who built a serious music career out of internet-era comedy.
Comedy songs with careful, genre-accurate production.

summary: Uncle Dave Macon was a banjo-playing showman and the first big star of the Grand Ole Opry, preserving a huge store of 19th-century songs on record.
know: He joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1926 and became its first featured star.
He ran a mule-drawn freight business before turning to music full time.
He was elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1966.
songs: Keep My Skillet Good and Greasy
Way Down the Old Plank Road

influenced.why: Acuff came up on the Opry in Macon's shadow and carried on his old-time showmanship.
Smith put several Macon recordings on the Anthology of American Folk Music.
Macon's recordings were part of the old-time banjo repertoire Seeger learned and spread.
Hartford's banjo-and-storytelling act drew directly on the old Opry songster tradition Macon embodied.
Their rowdy string-band revival plays the kind of old-time material Macon popularized.

cousins.why: A comic, larger-than-life entertainer who was also a serious musician.
A songster from the same early recording era who kept older songs alive.

summary: Gene Autry was the original singing cowboy, a record and film star who made western songs a national craze and recorded some of the best-selling Christmas songs ever.
know: He began as a Jimmie Rodgers-style singer billed as Oklahoma's Yodeling Cowboy on Tulsa radio.
His 1949 recording of "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" became one of the top-selling singles of its time.
He later owned the California Angels baseball team.

influencedBy.why: Autry started out closely imitating Rodgers's blue yodels before finding his cowboy style.

influenced.why: Robbins grew up on Autry's westerns and built his gunfighter ballads on that image.
Peck's masked singing cowboy persona draws on the Hollywood western image Autry created.

cousins.why: A fellow 1930s and 1940s crooner whose Christmas records became perennials.
Easygoing film-and-record star with a relaxed, friendly vocal style.

summary: Roy Acuff was the Grand Ole Opry's biggest star of the late 1930s and 1940s and, as a publisher, helped build Nashville into the country music business center.
know: He joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1938 and was long called the King of Country Music.
In 1942 he co-founded Acuff-Rose Publishing with songwriter Fred Rose, which later signed Hank Williams.
In 1962 he became the first living person elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame.

influencedBy.why: Macon was the Opry's elder star, and Acuff learned its showmanship and old-time repertoire alongside him.
Acuff's mountain gospel and sacred songs come from the same tradition the Carters put on record.

influenced.why: Hank idolized Acuff's emotional singing and was signed to Acuff-Rose, which published his songs.
The Louvins grew up on Acuff's Opry broadcasts and his mix of secular and sacred songs.
Acuff sang on their 1972 Will the Circle Be Unbroken sessions, linking his generation to theirs.

cousins.why: Gospel-rooted singing that crossed into popular music without losing its church feel.
Train songs and plain-voiced Depression-era singing for working people.

summary: Ernest Tubb was a Texas singer who helped define honky-tonk music in the 1940s, put electric guitar at the center of country records, and championed younger artists.
know: Jimmie Rodgers's widow helped launch his career and gave him one of Rodgers's guitars.
His 1941 hit "Walking the Floor Over You" was an early electric-guitar country smash.
He opened the Ernest Tubb Record Shop in Nashville in 1947 and hosted the Midnite Jamboree radio show from it.

influencedBy.why: Tubb began as a devoted Rodgers imitator, and Rodgers's widow personally helped him get started.
Texas dance-hall music shaped the steady, danceable beat of his honky-tonk records.

influenced.why: Tubb helped bring Snow to the Grand Ole Opry in 1950.
He championed Lynn early and recorded a string of hit duets with her in the 1960s.
Tubb's plain honky-tonk delivery was part of the sound Hank built on.
Jones came up on Tubb's Texas honky-tonk records and their jukebox style.

cousins.why: Simple, steady, instantly recognizable barroom records with plain singing.
Turned up the electric guitar in a rural style and made it the sound of the clubs.

summary: Ira and Charlie Louvin were a brother duo whose high, tight harmonies on gospel and heartbreak songs became a model for country and rock harmony singers.
know: Ira sang the high harmony and played mandolin, while Charlie sang lead and played guitar.
They joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1955.
Their 1959 gospel album Satan Is Real is famous for its homemade cover art.
songs: I Don't Believe You've Met My Baby

influencedBy.why: The Delmores set the pattern for the brother-duet harmony style the Louvins refined.
Monroe's high lonesome tenor and mandolin shaped Ira's singing and playing.
Much of their gospel and ballad repertoire comes from the Carter Family tradition.
They grew up on Acuff's Opry broadcasts mixing sacred and secular songs.

influenced.why: The Everlys modeled their harmony on the Louvins and later recorded an album of their songs.
Parsons championed the Louvins and recorded their songs throughout his career.
The Byrds recorded the Louvins' "The Christian Life" on Sweetheart of the Rodeo.
Harris had an early hit with the Louvins' "If I Could Only Win Your Love" in 1975.

cousins.why: Two-voice harmony as the heart of the sound.
Family harmony singing rooted in gospel.

summary: Lester Flatt and Earl Scruggs left Bill Monroe's band to form the Foggy Mountain Boys, and Scruggs's three-finger banjo made them bluegrass's most popular act.
know: Both played in Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys from about 1945 to 1948.
"The Ballad of Jed Clampett," the Beverly Hillbillies theme, was a number one country hit for them.
"Foggy Mountain Breakdown" was used in the 1967 film Bonnie and Clyde.
songs: Roll in My Sweet Baby's Arms

influencedBy.why: Both men were members of Monroe's band, where the classic bluegrass sound took shape.
They recorded Carter songs, and Maybelle Carter toured with them in the 1960s.

influenced.why: Skaggs played mandolin on their TV show as a young child and later revived their repertoire.
Fleck has said hearing the Beverly Hillbillies theme made him want to play banjo.
Earl Scruggs played on their Will the Circle Be Unbroken sessions.
Hartford's banjo style grew directly out of the Scruggs approach.
Jerry Garcia started as a Scruggs-style bluegrass banjo player.
Their drive and instrumental flash is the foundation of the bluegrass Strings plays.
Krauss came up in a bluegrass world shaped by their records and repertoire.

cousins.why: A virtuoso who invented a new way to play his instrument and made it lead.
Tight, instrument-led records that showcase a band's drive.

summary: Ralph Stanley co-led the Stanley Brothers and then the Clinch Mountain Boys, keeping a stark mountain style of bluegrass and singing alive for seven decades.
know: From 1967 he led the Clinch Mountain Boys on his own after years co-leading with his brother Carter.
His band was the starting point for Ricky Skaggs and Keith Whitley.
His unaccompanied "O Death" on the O Brother, Where Art Thou? soundtrack won him a Grammy in 2002.

influencedBy.why: His lifelong partnership with his brother Carter formed his whole style.
Monroe's new bluegrass sound shaped the early Stanley Brothers records.
Mountain ballads and gospel from the Carter tradition run through his repertoire.

influenced.why: Skaggs joined Stanley's band as a teenager.
Dylan named Stanley as a favorite and recorded a duet with him in the 1990s.
Burnett built the O Brother soundtrack around Stanley and later produced him.
Welch's spare Appalachian style draws directly on the Stanley sound.
Childers's eastern Kentucky mountain singing traces back to Stanley's style.
Strings came up playing the traditional bluegrass repertoire Stanley kept alive.

cousins.why: Raw, spiritual singing with almost no polish.
Sacred music sung with enormous intensity.

summary: Doc Watson was a North Carolina guitarist and singer whose fast, clean flatpicking of fiddle tunes changed how the acoustic guitar is played in folk and bluegrass.
know: He was brought to folk revival audiences in the early 1960s after folklorist Ralph Rinzler recorded him.
He toured and recorded for years with his son Merle, and MerleFest is named for Merle.
He named his son after guitarist Merle Travis.
keyAlbums: Will the Circle Be Unbroken (with Nitty Gritty Dirt Band)

influencedBy.why: Watson learned from Delmore Brothers records, and "Deep River Blues" became a signature tune.
Watson admired Travis enough to name his son after him and absorbed his fingerpicking.
Rodgers's records were among the first country music Watson heard and sang.
Many of his ballads and gospel songs come from the Carter Family repertoire.

influenced.why: Watson was a central guest on their Will the Circle Be Unbroken sessions.
Strings has named Watson as a major guitar hero and plays many of his tunes.
Watson's flatpicking set the bar for the newgrass virtuosity Fleck's generation pursued.

cousins.why: Overcame physical limits to become the defining guitarist of his style.
Gentle, rolling guitar and an unhurried voice on old songs.

summary: Kitty Wells was the first woman to top the country charts as a solo artist and opened the door for women singers in the male-dominated honky-tonk era.
know: "It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels" reached number one in 1952 as an answer song to Hank Thompson's "The Wild Side of Life."
She was billed as the Queen of Country Music.
She was married to Johnnie Wright of the duo Johnnie & Jack.
songs: It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels

influencedBy.why: Her plain, unornamented vocal style comes from the Carter Family's mountain singing.
She came up on the Opry sound Acuff defined.

influenced.why: Lynn has named Wells as her early idol and model.
Wells proved a woman could carry honky-tonk heartbreak songs to the top of the chart.
Wells was one of the women who made a solo country career like Parton's possible.

cousins.why: A woman who broke through in a field run by men and set a new standard.
A woman singer whose plain, direct delivery set the standard for heartbreak songs.

summary: Hank Snow was a Canadian singer and guitarist known as the Singing Ranger, whose fast-talking train songs made him one of country's biggest stars of the 1950s.
know: "I'm Movin' On" spent 21 weeks at number one on the country chart in 1950.
He named his son Jimmie Rodgers Snow after his hero.
His booking agency, run with Colonel Tom Parker, handled an early Elvis Presley tour.

influencedBy.why: Snow modeled himself on Rodgers and named his son after him.
Tubb sponsored his arrival on the Grand Ole Opry in 1950.

influenced.why: Presley toured on Snow's package shows and recorded songs from his catalog.
Cash recorded "I've Been Everywhere" and carried on the talking train-song style.
Charles recorded "I'm Movin' On," bringing Snow's song into R&B.
The Stones played "I'm Movin' On" in their early live sets.

cousins.why: Fast, rhythmic train and travel songs.
A Canadian storyteller with railroad songs at the core of his catalog.

summary: Marty Robbins was a versatile country singer best known for his cinematic gunfighter ballads, which brought western story songs back to the top of the charts.
know: "El Paso" won the first Grammy for best country and western recording.
The fuzz-tone guitar on "Don't Worry" came from a faulty amplifier during the session.
He also raced stock cars in NASCAR.
keyAlbums: More Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs

influencedBy.why: Robbins grew up on Autry's westerns, and they shaped his cowboy songs.
Rodgers's western and blue-yodel songs were part of his early repertoire.

influenced.why: The Dead played "El Paso" hundreds of times in concert.
Wall's cowboy story songs follow the gunfighter-ballad tradition Robbins made famous.
Peck's dramatic western crooning echoes Robbins's style.

cousins.why: Big, dramatic ballads sung with a soaring tenor.
A smooth crooner who could sell a story song.

summary: Jim Reeves was a velvet-voiced singer whose soft, close-miked ballads helped define the polished Nashville sound and made him a star around the world.
know: He worked as an announcer at KWKH, home of the Louisiana Hayride, before his singing career took off.
His RCA records were produced by Chet Atkins.
He was hugely popular abroad, including in the UK, Ireland, Norway and South Africa.

influencedBy.why: Reeves's relaxed, intimate crooning follows Crosby's microphone-based style.
Atkins produced his RCA hits and shaped their smooth arrangements.

cousins.why: A warm, intimate baritone that crossed every audience.
Easy, velvety ballads for a wide pop audience.

summary: Chet Atkins was a fingerstyle guitar master and the RCA executive and producer who, with Owen Bradley, built the smooth Nashville sound of the late 1950s and 1960s.
know: He ran RCA Victor's Nashville operation and signed artists including Charley Pride.
He played guitar on early RCA sessions for Elvis Presley.
Gretsch and later Gibson made signature Chet Atkins guitar models.

influencedBy.why: Atkins built his thumb-and-finger picking on Travis's style.
He admired Django's jazz guitar and borrowed from it.
Les Paul's tone and studio approach were a model for Atkins the guitarist and producer.
He played in Mother Maybelle and the Carter Sisters' band around 1950, which brought him to Nashville.

influenced.why: Atkins produced Reeves's RCA hits and shaped their soft, polished sound.
He played on and helped organize Presley's first RCA sessions.
He helped the Everlys get started and played on their early records.
He signed and produced Jennings's early RCA albums.
He signed Pride to RCA in 1965.
He produced Reed and recorded duet albums with him.
Mark Knopfler named Atkins as a hero and made a duet album with him.
George Harrison's early playing and Gretsch guitars came straight from his admiration of Atkins.

cousins.why: A producer who shaped a whole era's sound from inside a record company.
A musician-producer whose taste set a polished standard for a genre.

summary: Owen Bradley was the Decca Records producer who, with Chet Atkins, created the Nashville sound, making landmark records with Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn and Brenda Lee.
know: With his brother Harold he opened a studio on Nashville's 16th Avenue in the 1950s, the start of Music Row.
He headed Decca's Nashville division for years.
He came out of retirement to produce k.d. lang's Shadowland in 1988.

influenced.why: Bradley produced her biggest hits and framed her voice with strings and backing singers.
He produced Lynn's Decca records through her rise to stardom.
He produced Holly's 1956 Decca sessions in Nashville.
He produced Shadowland, her tribute to the Nashville sound.
Sherrill's lush countrypolitan productions extended the approach Bradley pioneered.

cousins.why: A record-company producer who defined the sound of the stars he recorded.
A producer known for a big, layered signature sound.

summary: Billy Sherrill was the Epic Records producer and songwriter behind the lush countrypolitan sound, making classic records with Tammy Wynette, George Jones and Charlie Rich.
know: He co-wrote "Stand by Your Man" with Tammy Wynette.
He produced George Jones's "He Stopped Loving Her Today."
He produced Elvis Costello's country album Almost Blue in 1981.
keyAlbums: I Am What I Am (George Jones)

influencedBy.why: Sherrill built his string-heavy style on the Nashville sound Bradley created.
His big, layered productions are often compared to Spector's wall of sound.

influenced.why: He signed her, produced her hits and co-wrote her signature song.
He produced Jones for two decades, including his most famous ballad.
He produced Costello's Almost Blue in Nashville.

cousins.why: A producer whose signature arrangements defined a label's sound.
Polished, big-budget productions that made stars of singers.

summary: Tammy Wynette was a country singer known as the First Lady of Country Music, whose aching voice on Billy Sherrill's lush productions made her one of the genre's defining stars.
know: She worked as a hairdresser before her music career took off.
"Stand by Your Man" became one of the best-selling singles by a woman in country history.
She recorded "Justified and Ancient" with the British group The KLF in 1991.
keyAlbums: Your Good Girl's Gonna Go Bad
songs: 'Til I Can Make It on My Own

influencedBy.why: Sherrill signed her, produced her records and co-wrote her biggest hit.
Her husband and duet partner, Jones shaped her phrasing on their many records together.
Wells set the model for a woman singing honky-tonk heartbreak.
Cline's emotional ballad singing in lush settings paved the way for her sound.

cousins.why: Big, emotional ballad singing that defined a genre's female voice.
Heartbreak songs sung over lush string arrangements.

summary: Charley Pride was a Mississippi-born baritone who became one of RCA's best-selling artists and country music's first Black superstar.
know: He played Negro league baseball, including for the Memphis Red Sox, before singing professionally.
Chet Atkins signed him to RCA in 1965.
In 2000 he became the first Black artist elected to the Country Music Hall of Fame.
songs: Is Anybody Goin' to San Antone
All I Have to Offer You (Is Me)

influencedBy.why: Pride grew up on Hank's records and kept his songs in his repertoire.
Atkins signed him to RCA and backed his career there.
He heard Tubb and other Opry stars on the radio growing up.

influenced.why: Pride's success is a reference point for Black artists in mainstream country like Brown.

cousins.why: Brought a soul singer's warmth to country songs.
A smooth baritone who broke barriers in a mainstream format.

summary: Glen Campbell was an in-demand Los Angeles session guitarist who became a crossover star singing Jimmy Webb songs like "Wichita Lineman" and "Galveston."
know: As part of the Wrecking Crew he played guitar on records by the Beach Boys, Frank Sinatra and many others.
He filled in for Brian Wilson on Beach Boys tours in the mid-1960s.
He hosted The Glen Campbell Goodtime Hour on TV from 1969 to 1972.
keyAlbums: By the Time I Get to Phoenix
songs: By the Time I Get to Phoenix

influencedBy.why: Campbell often named Django as his favorite guitarist.
His years in the Wrecking Crew taught him studio craft and pop arranging.

influenced.why: He played guitar on Beach Boys sessions and toured with them.
Campbell helped Jackson get his first publishing deal in Nashville.

cousins.why: Lush, orchestral pop ballads sung with a clear, emotional voice.
Sophisticated pop songcraft with strings and unusual chord changes.

summary: Roger Miller was a witty singer-songwriter whose playful mid-1960s hits like "King of the Road" made him a pop star and a Grammy record-setter.
know: He won 11 Grammys across 1965 and 1966.
He wrote the songs for the Broadway musical Big River, which won the Tony for best score in 1985.
He voiced the rooster narrator in Disney's 1973 Robin Hood.

influencedBy.why: Miller grew up on Hank and started as a Nashville writer in the plain honky-tonk tradition.
He grew up in Oklahoma on western swing and kept its loose, playful rhythm.

cousins.why: Clever wordplay and comic timing in short, catchy songs.
A jokey, swinging entertainer who was also a sharp musician.

summary: Bobbie Gentry was a Mississippi-born singer-songwriter whose mysterious story song "Ode to Billie Joe" made her a star and who wrote and produced much of her own work.
know: She won three Grammys in 1968, including best new artist.
She produced much of her own material, which was rare for a woman at the time.
She recorded a hit duet album with Glen Campbell in 1968.

influenced.why: McEntire had one of her signature hits with Gentry's "Fancy."

cousins.why: Southern-tinged soul-pop sung with cool restraint.
Cinematic, atmospheric storytelling with a mysterious persona.

summary: Kris Kristofferson was a Rhodes Scholar turned Nashville songwriter whose literate songs changed what country lyrics could be and who became a film star.
know: He studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar before moving to Nashville.
He worked as a janitor at Columbia's Nashville studios while trying to sell his songs.
He was a member of the Highwaymen with Johnny Cash, Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings.
keyAlbums: The Silver Tongued Devil and I
songs: Help Me Make It Through the Night

influencedBy.why: Kristofferson often named Hank as the songwriter who drew him to country.
Cash championed him, recorded his songs and later shared the stage in the Highwaymen.
He cited Dylan as the model for writing poetic lyrics within popular song.

influenced.why: Kristofferson championed Prine early and helped bring him to wider attention.
Joplin's recording of his "Me and Bobby McGee" became her best-known song.
He produced Shaver's debut album.
Nelson recorded a whole album of his songs and joined him in the Highwaymen.
Isbell's detailed, literate country songwriting follows the path Kristofferson opened.

cousins.why: A poet who became a songwriter, with a deep, worn voice.
Working-class characters drawn with literary detail.

summary: David Allan Coe is an outlaw country singer and songwriter known for his rowdy honky-tonk records and for writing hits for other artists.
know: He wrote "Would You Lay with Me (In a Field of Stone)," a number one hit for Tanya Tucker.
He wrote "Take This Job and Shove It," a hit for Johnny Paycheck.
Early in his career he was billed as the Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy.
songs: You Never Even Called Me by My Name
Would You Lay with Me (In a Field of Stone)

influencedBy.why: Coe's honky-tonk style and song themes return to Hank Williams again and again.
He came up alongside the outlaw movement Waylon led.
Willie's outlaw independence is a direct model, named in his own songs.

cousins.why: Southern rock with a rough honky-tonk attitude.
Bearded Texas-style showmen with a raw roots sound.

summary: Jerry Jeff Walker was a New York-born folk singer who wrote "Mr. Bojangles" and became a central figure in the loose, good-time Austin progressive country scene of the 1970s.
know: He wrote "Mr. Bojangles," which the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band made a hit in 1970.
¡Viva Terlingua! was recorded live in the old dance hall in Luckenbach, Texas, in 1973.
His backing group was called the Lost Gonzo Band.
songs: Up Against the Wall, Redneck Mother

influencedBy.why: Walker started as a wandering folk singer in the Guthrie mold.
Dylan's Greenwich Village folk scene was the world Walker came out of.
His close friend Clark supplied several of his best-known songs.

influenced.why: Their hit version of "Mr. Bojangles" came from his song.

cousins.why: Loose, warm roots music played by a road-tested band.
Easygoing live shows built on community and long jams.

summary: Guy Clark was a Texas songwriter whose carefully crafted, detail-rich songs made him a mentor to generations of country and Americana writers.
know: He built guitars by hand and worked as a luthier.
He was a mentor to younger writers including Steve Earle and Rodney Crowell.
My Favorite Picture of You won the Grammy for best folk album.

influencedBy.why: Van Zandt was his close friend and the songwriter he most measured himself against.
Clark saw Hopkins in Houston clubs and cited him as a formative influence.
His plain-spoken narrative songs come out of the folk tradition Guthrie shaped.

influenced.why: Earle has called Clark one of his two main mentors.
Harris sang on Old No. 1 and recorded his songs.
Walker had some of his best-known recordings with Clark's songs.
Lovett has cited Clark as a model and recorded his songs.
Isbell's precise, detail-driven songwriting follows Clark's school.

cousins.why: Plain-spoken working-life songs told with exact detail.
A Texas songwriter's songwriter with a long, independent career.

summary: Billy Joe Shaver was a Texas songwriter whose songs formed the backbone of Waylon Jennings's Honky Tonk Heroes and helped define outlaw country.
know: He wrote nearly all the songs on Waylon Jennings's 1973 album Honky Tonk Heroes.
His debut album was produced by Kris Kristofferson.
In the 1990s he recorded and toured with his son Eddy, a guitarist, in the band Shaver.

songs: Old Five and Dimers Like Me

influencedBy.why: His plain honky-tonk writing and singing grow straight out of Hank Williams.
Kristofferson produced his debut album and championed his songs.

influenced.why: Shaver wrote almost the entire Honky Tonk Heroes album for Jennings.
Childers's plainspoken, autobiographical country writing follows Shaver's style.
Simpson's return to hard outlaw country draws on the Honky Tonk Heroes sound.

cousins.why: Texas songs about hard living, told in a conversational voice.
Rough-voiced storyteller with an eye for down-and-out characters.

summary: The Flying Burrito Brothers, formed by ex-Byrds Gram Parsons and Chris Hillman, fused hard country with rock and soul and laid the foundation for country rock and alt-country.

influencedBy.why: Parsons co-founded the band and wrote much of its material.
Founders Parsons and Hillman came straight from the Byrds' Sweetheart of the Rodeo lineup.
Bakersfield country's twang and drive shaped their sound.
Haggard's Bakersfield records were a key model for their hard country side.
Parsons loved the Louvins' close harmonies and gospel songs.
Their two-part harmonies drew on the Everly style.

influenced.why: Burrito member Bernie Leadon was a founding Eagle, carrying their country rock into the 1970s mainstream.
Their sound shaped the country rock Harris built with Parsons.
Uncle Tupelo's alt-country blend of punk and twang traces back to the Burritos.
The Jayhawks' harmony-heavy country rock follows the Burritos' template.
Wilco's early country rock comes out of the line the Burritos started.

cousins.why: Rock musicians reworking American roots styles.
Rock built on country and swamp roots.

summary: The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band began as a California jug band and became a bridge between generations with Will the Circle Be Unbroken, which joined them with country's founding figures.

influencedBy.why: Maybelle Carter played on Will the Circle Be Unbroken, and the title song is a Carter staple.

Watson was a central guest on Will the Circle Be Unbroken.
Travis played and told stories on the Circle sessions.
Their biggest early hit was Walker's "Mr. Bojangles."

cousins.why: A rock band reconnecting with older American music.
Roots-minded rock with folk and country underneath.

summary: Linda Ronstadt was one of the best-selling singers of the 1970s, a powerful interpreter who moved from Los Angeles country rock to pop, standards and Mexican music.
know: She first recorded with the folk-rock group the Stone Poneys, who had a hit with "Different Drum."

Her close friend and harmony partner, with whom she recorded Trio.
Her hit "Blue Bayou" came from Orbison's songbook.
She recorded his songs and drew on classic country ballad singing.

influenced.why: Founding Eagles Glenn Frey and Don Henley met as members of her backing band.
The Chicks' pop-crossover country with strong harmonies follows her example.
